newsitem.title: USA: Raytheon board meets amid talk of strategic shift.
newsitem.headline: Raytheon board meets amid talk of strategic shift.

text.p: Raytheon Corp's board of directors met on Wednesday amid speculation that the company will decide either to boost its defense operations through an acquisition or focus exclusively on its diversified commercial businesses.
Raytheon spokesman Robert McWade said the company's board convened at its headquarters in Lexington, Mass. He declined to disclose the meeting's agenda.

Analysts said every aspect of the company's future was likely to be discussed. The meeting follows the announcement last weekend of the planned merger between rivals Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp and the loss last Friday of a major missile contract with the U.S. military.

"The possibliites are almost endless," said Peter Aseritis, an analyst with First Boston. "They range from doing nothing to putting the company up for sale. I do think the board will have somewhat of a sense of urgency they didn't have in the past."
Raytheon Chief Executive Dennis Picard told analysts this autumn that the company was considering acquisitions to boost its defense business. He said Raytheon was not thinking of selling assets.

In addition to its defense business, Raytheon owns the Amana appliance company, a major construction business and a commercial aircraft division and other businesses. Together the commercial businesses accounted for about 60 percent of its $11.7 billion in sales in fiscal 1995.

Meanwhile, Hughes Electronics Corp, the defense unit of General Motors Corp, is up for sale. Analysts believe Raytheon and Northrop Grumman Corp will emerge as the top bidders for the business, valued at about $6 billion.
"I would think Northrop and Raytheon would be the most likely," Aseritis said. "I don't think Lockheed Martin Corp is going to bid."
A smaller target for Raytheon might be Texas Instruments Inc's $2 billion defense business, which is also up for sale, according to published reports.
Beyond that, a merger with rival Northrop Gruman is a possibility, or Raytheon could sell its defense operations and focus on its commercial businesses, analysts said.
The one scenario that Aseritis thinks is most unlikely is for Raytheon to maintain the status quo.

"If they stay where they are, they will probably get closed out of competition and get smaller and smaller," he said "I don't think they have that choice. If they want to stay in defense, I think they have to grow."
